explanations.explanation: Frogs it is! The LORD tells Moses, Israel's leader, to warn Pharaoh, Egypt's king, that refusing means frogs across his whole country. Not one pond of them. The WHOLE country. Friend, that's a warning with a lot of hop in it.

Locusts are a fair guess, but that's not the word in this warning. The LORD tells Moses, Israel's leader, what to say to Pharaoh, Egypt's king: “…I will plague your whole country with frogs.” (Exodus 8:2) Keep your eyes on the frogs, baker. They're about to be very busy.

Flies aren't what the LORD names here. In His message to Pharaoh, Egypt's king, He says, “…I will plague your whole country with frogs.” (Exodus 8:2) Whole country, friend. No corner of Egypt gets left out of that warning.

explanations.answer: Into their ovens and kneading bowls
explanations.explanation: Ovens and kneading bowls, yes! The LORD says the frogs will come “…and into your ovens and kneading bowls.” (Exodus 8:3) Friend, those are the places I do my best work, so this one hits close to the bakery. A frog in the dough is not on any recipe I know.

explanations.answer: Into their grain storehouses and barns
explanations.explanation: Storehouses and barns aren't on the list. What the LORD says is that the frogs will come “…and into your ovens and kneading bowls.” (Exodus 8:3) That's right inside the kitchen. These frogs have no respect for the cooking area.

explanations.answer: Into their wells and water jars
explanations.explanation: Wells and water jars aren't named in this warning. The LORD says the frogs will come “…and into your ovens and kneading bowls.” (Exodus 8:3) That puts them right in the middle of the baking. As a stamper, I take that personally.

Here's what the text actually says: “But the magicians did the same thing by their magic arts, and they also brought frogs up onto the land of Egypt.” (Exodus 8:7) So they did copy it. Egypt is already covered in frogs, and they show up and add MORE. Friend, I'd have kept my hands in my pockets.

Right, it's False. The text says, “But the magicians did the same thing by their magic arts, and they also brought frogs up onto the land of Egypt.” (Exodus 8:7) They did the same thing as Aaron, Moses' brother. Land already covered in frogs, and their big move is more frogs. Keep that in mind, because the story doesn't stop here.

explanations.answer: Pray to the LORD to take the frogs away
explanations.explanation: That's it. Pharaoh, Egypt's king, tells Moses and Aaron, “Pray to the LORD to take the frogs away from me and my people.” (Exodus 8:8) He's asking them to pray to the LORD. I think a king who can order anybody around knows this one is out of his hands.

explanations.answer: Strike the river with the staff again
explanations.explanation: No staff this time. Pharaoh, Egypt's king, asks for something else: “Pray to the LORD to take the frogs away from me and my people.” (Exodus 8:8) He wants the frogs gone, so he's asking for prayer. Moses, Israel's leader, and his brother Aaron are the ones he calls in to do it.

explanations.answer: Order the frogs out of the palace
explanations.explanation: Pharaoh, Egypt's king, doesn't give the frogs orders. He summons Moses and Aaron and says, “Pray to the LORD to take the frogs away from me and my people.” (Exodus 8:8) So he's asking Moses, Israel's leader, to pray to the LORD about it. A king asking for a prayer request, friend. That tells you how the frog situation is going.

True! Pharaoh, Egypt's king, says, “Then I will let your people go, that they may sacrifice to the LORD.” (Exodus 8:8) That's a real promise, right there on the table. Hold onto it, baker, because the story will test it.

It's True, actually. Pharaoh, Egypt's king, tells Moses and Aaron, “Then I will let your people go, that they may sacrifice to the LORD.” (Exodus 8:8) He puts it right after asking them to pray about the frogs. So the offer is on the table. Keep an eye on what he does with it.

Tomorrow! Pharaoh, Egypt's king, answers Moses, “Tomorrow.” (Exodus 8:10) Frogs in his palace, his bedroom and his bed, and he picks tomorrow. Friend, I'd have said "tonight, please, I'll hold the door myself."

Right now sounds like the smart pick, but that's not what Pharaoh, Egypt's king, says. When Moses, Israel's leader, asks when, Pharaoh answers, “Tomorrow.” (Exodus 8:10) He picks the next day. I'd have picked sooner, friend, and I wouldn't have let the question finish.

Sunset is a decent guess, but the text gives one word. When Moses, Israel's leader, asks Pharaoh, Egypt's king, when to pray, Pharaoh answers, “Tomorrow.” (Exodus 8:10) No hour is given. Just tomorrow, baker.

explanations.answer: There is no one like the LORD our God
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Moses, Israel's leader, replies, “May it be as you say… so that you may know that there is no one like the LORD our God.” (Exodus 8:10) Moses tells Pharaoh, Egypt's king, what the answer is meant to show. It points straight at the LORD, and Moses isn't pointing at himself.

explanations.answer: Moses is a servant of the LORD our God
explanations.explanation: That's not what Moses says. Moses, Israel's leader, tells Pharaoh, Egypt's king, “so that you may know that there is no one like the LORD our God.” (Exodus 8:10) He's pointing at who the LORD is. Moses doesn't say a word about himself in that line.

explanations.answer: The land of Egypt belongs to the LORD
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't say that here. He tells Pharaoh, Egypt's king, “so that you may know that there is no one like the LORD our God.” (Exodus 8:10) That's the reason he gives for agreeing to tomorrow. It's all about who the LORD is.

Close, but there's a catch. Moses, Israel's leader, says the frogs will leave Pharaoh's houses, officials and people, and then adds, “they will remain only in the Nile.” (Exodus 8:11) So the frogs in the river stay put. He even makes that exception when he asks Pharaoh, Egypt's king, about the timing (Exodus 8:9).

False is right. Moses, Israel's leader, tells Pharaoh, Egypt's king, that the frogs will leave his houses, his officials and his people, but “they will remain only in the Nile.” (Exodus 8:11) The river keeps its frogs. Friend, that's a very specific promise, and it's good to catch the small print.

They all die. The LORD does as Moses, Israel's leader, requested, and the frogs in the houses, the courtyards and the fields die (Exodus 8:13). It's a heavy picture, so I'll say it plain. The next verse shows how many there were: countless heaps.

explanations.answer: They hop back into the Nile
explanations.explanation: No hopping home. The text says the LORD did as Moses, Israel's leader, requested, and “…the frogs in the houses, the courtyards, and the fields died.” (Exodus 8:13) The next verse says they were piled into heaps. It's a heavy moment, baker, so let's treat it that way.

There's no wind in this passage. After Moses, Israel's leader, cries out, the LORD does as he requested, and “…the frogs in the houses, the courtyards, and the fields died.” (Exodus 8:13) That's what happens to them. It's a heavy part of the story, and I won't pretend otherwise.

Hardens. Pharaoh, Egypt's king, sees there's relief, and then “…he hardened his heart and would not listen to Moses and Aaron…” (Exodus 8:15) The frogs are gone, and so is the promise he made. Friend, the relief arrived and the listening left.

Softening would have changed the whole story, but it's not what happens. When Pharaoh, Egypt's king, sees there's relief, “…he hardened his heart and would not listen to Moses and Aaron…” (Exodus 8:15) Moses is Israel's leader, and Aaron is his brother. Pharaoh dug in instead.

Guards is a clever pick, but the text uses a different word. When Pharaoh, Egypt's king, sees there's relief, “…he hardened his heart and would not listen to Moses and Aaron…” (Exodus 8:15) Hardened, baker. It's the word to remember from this part of the story.

True. Pharaoh, Egypt's king, “…hardened his heart and would not listen to Moses and Aaron, just as the LORD had said.” (Exodus 8:15) The text says the LORD had said it. So it happens exactly the way He told them.

Ohh, this one's a trick, baker. It's True. Pharaoh, Egypt's king, “…hardened his heart and would not listen to Moses and Aaron, just as the LORD had said.” (Exodus 8:15) Aaron is Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14). The frogs die, the relief comes, and Pharaoh's whole attitude is, "Okay, we're good now." We're NOT good, Pharaoh! I once told myself I'd clean out the junk drawer 'tomorrow,' too, so I know how fast a promise goes when the pressure's off.

The dust! The LORD tells Moses, Israel's leader, to say to Aaron, “Stretch out your staff and strike the dust of the earth…” (Exodus 8:16) Not water this time. Just plain ground-level dust. Then verse 17 says all the dust of the earth turned into gnats throughout the land of Egypt. Friend, I've swept up plenty of dust, and I never once checked it for gnats.

Not the Nile this time. The LORD tells Moses, Israel's leader, to say to Aaron, “Stretch out your staff and strike the dust of the earth…” (Exodus 8:16) Aaron is Moses' brother, and the staff is going to the ground. The target changes, so it's good to catch it.

No rock in this passage. The LORD tells Moses, Israel's leader, to say to Aaron, “Stretch out your staff and strike the dust of the earth…” (Exodus 8:16) Aaron is Moses' brother. The staff hits the dust, and then the text says gnats came upon man and beast (Exodus 8:17).

Gnats! The LORD says the strike is so “…that it may turn into swarms of gnats throughout the land of Egypt.” (Exodus 8:16) Dust becomes gnats. Friend, I've been annoyed by one gnat at a time, and this is SWARMS.

Hornets would be a rough day, but that's not the word here. The LORD says the dust will turn into “…swarms of gnats throughout the land of Egypt.” (Exodus 8:16) Gnats, baker. Small, but there are swarms of them.

Bees are a fair guess, but the text says something else. The LORD tells Moses, Israel's leader, that the dust will turn into “…swarms of gnats throughout the land of Egypt.” (Exodus 8:16) Gnats, throughout the whole land. No bees in this passage.

They can't make any. The text says, “The magicians tried to produce gnats using their magic arts, but they could not.” (Exodus 8:18) They matched the frogs, and now they've hit a wall. Friend, that's a long way from "let me add some more."

More gnats would be the frog story all over again, but that's not what happens. The text says, “The magicians tried to produce gnats using their magic arts, but they could not.” (Exodus 8:18) They try, and nothing comes. This time they can't match it.

explanations.answer: They make only a few gnats
explanations.explanation: Not even a few. The text says, “The magicians tried to produce gnats using their magic arts, but they could not.” (Exodus 8:18) Zero gnats from them, while the gnats Aaron's staff brought stayed on man and beast. They came up empty, baker.

explanations.answer: This is the finger of God
explanations.explanation: That's what they say. “This is the finger of God…” the magicians tell Pharaoh, Egypt's king. (Exodus 8:19) These are the same magicians who did the same thing with the frogs, so that line is quite something. They called it the finger of God.

explanations.answer: This is the staff of Aaron
explanations.explanation: They don't say that. The magicians tell Pharaoh, Egypt's king, “This is the finger of God…” (Exodus 8:19) Aaron, Moses' brother, is the one who struck the dust with the staff, but the magicians' words are about God. They point past the people, baker.

explanations.answer: This is the hand of Moses
explanations.explanation: That's not their line. The magicians tell Pharaoh, Egypt's king, “This is the finger of God…” (Exodus 8:19) Moses is Israel's leader, but they don't name him. They name God.

Not quite. The text says, “But Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said.” (Exodus 8:19) The magicians speak up, and Pharaoh, Egypt's king, doesn't listen. Same as with Moses and Aaron.

False is right. The text says, “But Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said.” (Exodus 8:19) His own magicians say, “This is the finger of God…” and Pharaoh, Egypt's king, still won't listen. Friend, even that doesn't move him.
